verses.text: Now there were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you. They will secretly introduce destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them—bringing swift destruction on themselves.
Many will follow in their depravity, and because of them the way of truth will be defamed.
In their greed, these false teachers will exploit you with deceptive words. The longstanding verdict against them remains in force, and their destruction does not sleep.
For if God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them deep into hell, placing them in chains of darkness to be held for judgment;
if He did not spare the ancient world when He brought the flood on its ungodly people, but preserved Noah, a preacher of righteousness, among the eight;
if He condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to destruction, reducing them to ashes as an example of what is coming on the ungodly;
and if He rescued Lot, a righteous man distressed by the depraved conduct of the lawless
(for that righteous man, living among them day after day, was tormented in his righteous soul by the lawless deeds he saw and heard)—
if all this is so, then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to hold the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment.
Such punishment is specially reserved for those who indulge the corrupt desires of the flesh and despise authority. Bold and self-willed, they are unafraid to slander glorious beings.
Yet not even angels, though greater in strength and power, dare to bring such slanderous charges against them before the Lord.
These men are like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be captured and destroyed. They blaspheme in matters they do not understand, and like such creatures, they too will be destroyed.
The harm they will suffer is the wages of their wickedness. They consider it a pleasure to carouse in broad daylight. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deception as they feast with you.
Their eyes are full of adultery; their desire for sin is never satisfied; they seduce the unstable. They are accursed children with hearts trained in greed.
They have left the straight way and wandered off to follow the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness.
But he was rebuked for his transgression by a donkey, otherwise without speech, that spoke with a man's voice and restrained the prophet's madness.
These men are springs without water and mists driven by a storm. Blackest darkness is reserved for them.
With lofty but empty words, they appeal to the sensual passions of the flesh and entice those who are just escaping from others who live in error.
They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity. For a man is a slave to whatever has mastered him.

If indeed they have escaped the corruption of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, only to be entangled and overcome by it again, their final condition is worse than it was at first.
It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than to have known it and then to turn away from the holy commandment passed on to them.
Of them the proverbs are true: "A dog returns to its vomit," and, "A sow that is washed goes back to her wallowing in the mud."

context.author: Simon Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ (1:1); the authorship is debated.
context.audience: The same churches as in chapter 1, warned about teachers who will arise among them (2:1).
context.setting: Peter warns that false teachers will secretly bring in destructive heresies, denying the Master who bought them. Using Old Testament examples (fallen angels, Noah’s flood, Sodom and Gomorrah, Lot), he shows that God knows how to rescue the godly and keep the unrighteous under punishment.
context.custom: Balaam’s love of pay is the model for the false teachers (2:15). The first of the two sayings in 2:22 is Proverbs 26:11; the second, about a washed sow, is not found in the Old Testament. Springs without water (2:17) would disappoint a traveler in a dry land.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 3 answers the scoffers who mock the promise of Christ’s coming.
context.timelineBible: Peter draws on Genesis 6-8 and 19, Numbers 22-24 and Proverbs 26:11. This chapter runs close to Jude 4-18, and most scholars think 2 Peter used Jude.
context.sparkNotes: There will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies. Many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. God did not spare the angels when they sinned, nor the ancient world, but protected Noah. He turned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes, but rescued righteous Lot. The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to keep the unrighteous under punishment. These men are waterless springs. They promise freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption.

translation.meaning: Destruction, ruin. Their heresies lead to ruin.
Purchased at a market. They deny the Master who bought them.

otBackground.note: The sons of God and the daughters of men.

overview.summary: False teachers will arise with greed and sensuality. God judged fallen angels, the flood generation, and Sodom, and will judge them too.
overview.settingLine: Peter writes near the end of his life.

history.t: Numbers 22-24 tells how the king of Moab hired Balaam son of Beor to curse Israel, and how his donkey spoke to him. Numbers 31:16 blames his advice for Israel’s sin at Peor. Peter says the false teachers follow his way because he “loved the wages of wickedness” (2:15-16). Jude 11 also names Balaam.

Peter says God condemned Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes as an example, and rescued Lot (2:6-8). Genesis 19 tells the story. Peter calls Lot righteous, a word Genesis does not use of him, and Jesus joined the days of Noah and the days of Lot (Luke 17:26-30).

Verse 4 says God did not spare the angels who sinned but put them in chains of darkness until the judgment. The Greek verb takes them to Tartarus, the prison of the underworld in Greek myth. Most readers link the verse to Genesis 6:1-4 and the Book of Enoch, and Jude 6 says almost the same thing.

customs.t: In a dry land a spring was where a traveler expected to drink. Peter says the false teachers are springs without water and mists driven by a storm (2:17): they promise refreshment and give none.

Dogs in the Bible are usually scavengers, not pets, and pigs were unclean for Jews. Peter closes the chapter with two sayings: a dog returns to its vomit (Proverbs 26:11), and a washed sow goes back to wallowing in the mud (2:22).
Peter says they count it a pleasure to revel in the daytime and to feast with the believers (2:13). Drinking and feasting belonged to the evening, as Acts 2:15 and 1 Thessalonians 5:7 assume.

archaeology.t: In 1967 an expedition at Tell Deir ’Alla in the Jordan valley found plaster wall fragments written in ink, about 800 BC, that begin as the book of Balaam son of Beor, a seer. The name is the same as in Numbers 22-24, though the text does not mention Israel or a donkey. The picture here is a modern transcription of part of the text, not the plaster itself.

Bab edh-Dhra is a walled Early Bronze Age town east of the Dead Sea, beside a very large cemetery with buildings for bones. It is one of the candidate sites for Sodom. No inscription names Sodom there, its date (about 3300-2350 BC) is earlier than most dates given for Abraham, and other scholars favor other sites.

Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, from Nineveh, tells of a flood survivor who builds a boat. Scholars compare it with Genesis 6-9. Peter says only that God preserved Noah, a preacher of righteousness, when he brought the flood on the ungodly world (2:5).

overview.discussion: Peter warns that people promise freedom but are enslaved themselves. What “freedom” offered by culture might actually lead to slavery?
overview.book: The second letter of Peter · 3 chapters. Peter’s last words, written as he expects to die soon.
overview.author: Peter
overview.audience: The same believers as the first letter
